Tactic dependency-hygiene: Dependency Hygiene
    Name: Dependency Hygiene
    Purpose: Keep a project's dependency tree free of known vulnerabilities and non-compliant licenses. Apply at project creation, when adding any dependency, and as part of regular pre-release maintenance. Apply when: starting a new project, adding or upgrading any dependency, a vulnerability scanner reports new CVEs, or preparing a release. For JavaScript/TypeScript projects specifically, dependency hygiene also covers install-time supply-chain safety (registry authenticity, package freshness, lifecycle-script discipline, lockfile behavior, and Node runtime baseline) per the supply-chain-install-safety directive and tactic — see the JS/TS-specific steps below.
    Steps:
      - Pin all direct dependency versions explicitly
        Every direct dependency must have an explicit version declared in a central properties or constraints block. Never rely on inherited or transitive version resolution for direct dependencies; implicit resolution hides future breakage.
      - Import BOMs before declaring overrides (Java/Maven)
        Import BOM dependencies at the top of dependencyManagement, before any version overrides. This ensures your explicit pins take precedence over BOM-managed transitive versions. Document the reason for each version override.
      - Audit and exclude vulnerable transitives
        Identify vulnerable transitive dependencies and exclude them explicitly. Do not rely on upgrades of parent components to resolve transitive CVEs. For each exclusion, add a comment explaining the CVE or vulnerability motivation.
      - Restrict dependency resolution to approved registries
        Explicitly configure the build tool to resolve only from approved registries (e.g., Maven Central, PyPI). Unintended resolution from unapproved registries is a supply-chain risk.
      - Audit license compliance before adding a dependency
        Before adding any new component, verify its license. Permissive licenses (Apache 2.0, MIT, BSD-3-Clause) are typically safe. Limited-copyleft licenses (LGPL, MPL, EPL) require evaluation. Strong-copyleft licenses (GPL-2.0, GPL-3.0) require explicit approval. Document the license decision in an ADR or comment when the choice is non-obvious.
      - Run the dependency update report periodically
        At least once per release cycle, run a full outdated-dependency report. Prioritize upgrades for components with known CVEs. Read the component's changelog before upgrading to detect API incompatibilities.
      - Regenerate the SBOM after any dependency change
        After adding, removing, or upgrading any dependency, regenerate the Software Bill of Materials and commit it. SBOM drift causes silent gaps in vulnerability tracking.
      - JS/TS — verify registry authenticity before adding a package
        For JavaScript/TypeScript projects, confirm that any new or changed npm dependency resolves on the official registry (registry.npmjs.org, or an organization's approved private registry/proxy) and not an unexpected mirror or namespace. Do not accept a resolution that lands on an unfamiliar registry URL without explicit operator attention.
      - JS/TS — report package freshness before accepting a version
        Surface first-publish and latest-publish/update timestamps for the resolved package version before accepting it. A version published very recently, or during a known active incident window, is a risk signal that must be visible to the operator, not silently accepted.
      - JS/TS — deny-by-default lifecycle script execution
        Treat `preinstall`/`install`/`postinstall` scripts as deny-by-default for every new or changed npm/yarn/pnpm dependency. Do not globally disable script safety (e.g. blanket `--ignore-scripts` bypass configured back to "on") to work around a legitimate build need. When a lifecycle script is genuinely required (native module builds), add an explicit, scoped allowlist entry with the justification documented alongside the change.
      - JS/TS — confirm lockfile-driven, reproducible installs
        Commit and rely on the ecosystem lockfile (package-lock.json, yarn.lock, or pnpm-lock.yaml) for reproducible installs, and use the frozen/CI install mode in automation so an unreviewed dependency-tree change cannot silently slip into a build. Review lockfile diffs the same way manifest diffs are reviewed — a lockfile-only change can still introduce a new transitive dependency or resolve to a different version.
      - JS/TS — check the Node runtime baseline
        Check the project's declared/runtime Node version against the current Active LTS line. If the project intentionally runs a non-LTS or outdated Node version, document the business rationale explicitly rather than leaving the skew unacknowledged; do not silently accept an outdated baseline.
